entry.title: Traffic, Reaction Time, and Green Lights

link.title: Traffic, Reaction Time, and Green Lights

entry.content:
Growing up in the Bay Area, I have spent an unfortunate amount of time stuck in traffic. This has shaped my current views on cars, driving, and city planning. I might talk about this further in another post, but for now I will leave you with the trailer for the YouTube channel Not Just Bikes: link. It should go without saying that I do not agree with everything he says, though there is certainly a lot I do agree with.

On one of my trips back to San Jose from New York, while sitting at a traffic light, I had the following question:

How does reaction time affect the number of cars that get through during a green light?

At some point (while not driving) I got around to formulating this mathematically and got a clean, simple formula, which is what this post is about. Here is the setup to our problem:

  1. We observe one lane of traffic with an indefinite number of cars waiting in line.
  2. Each car is identical and of length $L$ meters.
  3. The light stays green for $T$ seconds.
  4. There is no space between cars.
  5. Each driver has a reaction time of $ au$ seconds. The driver at the front reacts to the light turning green and each subsequent driver reacts to the car in front of them starting to move.
  6. Each car moves at constant acceleration $a$ meters/second^2.
  7. Let $x_0$ denote the initial position of the first car’s front bumper. We say that car $n$ has made the light if its back bumper reaches $x_0$. Since there are no gaps between cars, this requires the car in the $n$th position to travel a distance of $nL$ meters within the $T$ seconds that the light is green.

We want to derive $N( au)$, the number of cars that pass through the intersection as a function of reaction time.

Unlimited acceleration

The train benchmark

Let’s first consider the idealized scenario where each driver has a perfect reaction time, i.e., $ au = 0$. Then the cars essentially form a train, accelerating synchronously as soon as the light turns green. How many cars will pass through in this case? It will simply be how far the train travels in $T$ seconds at constant acceleration $a$ divided by the length of each car, rounded down to the nearest integer: egin{equation} N_{\mathrm{train}} = \left\lfloor rac{a T^2}{2L} ight floor, \end{equation} where we obtained the distance traveled via kinematics. This gives us the upper bound on how many cars will pass through and it will be interesting to compare with the nonzero $ au$ case which we derive now.

Including reaction time

Observe that car $n$ gets through if the following condition is met: [total reaction time delay caused by the $(n-1)$ cars in front of car $n$ and its own reaction time delay] + [time $t$ it takes car $n$ to travel distance $nL$] $\leq T$. The first term is simply $(n-1) au + au = n au$. The second term is found via kinematics. We have egin{align} nL &= rac{1}{2}a t^2 ewline \implies t &= \sqrt{ rac{2nL}{a}}. \end{align} Putting things together, the mathematical condition for the $n$th car to pass through is given by egin{equation} n au + \sqrt{ rac{2nL}{a}} \leq T. \end{equation} Let $m = \sqrt{n}$. Then we have egin{equation} au m^2 + \sqrt{ rac{2L}{a}} m - T \leq 0. \end{equation} We want to find the maximal $m$ that satisfies this inequality because its square will give the continuous threshold for $n$. Denote this maximal $m$ by $M( au)$. For $ au>0$, using the quadratic formula and discarding the negative root gives egin{align} M( au) &= rac{\sqrt{ rac{2L}{a} +4 au T} - \sqrt{ rac{2L}{a}}}{2 au}. \end{align} Squaring $M( au)$ gives the continuous throughput threshold. Let egin{equation} \widetilde{N}( au) = M( au)^2 = \left( rac{\sqrt{ rac{2L}{a} +4 au T} - \sqrt{ rac{2L}{a}}}{2 au} ight)^2. \end{equation} The actual number of cars must be an integer, so we round this threshold down: egin{equation} N( au) = \left\lfloor \widetilde{N}( au) ight floor. \end{equation} As a sanity check, we would want to verify that the expression before rounding reduces to the train result when $ au o 0$. By using L’Hôpital’s rule, we do indeed find that egin{equation} \lim_{ au o 0} \widetilde{N}( au) = rac{a T^2}{2L}. \end{equation} Therefore, at exactly $ au=0$, we recover $N(0)=N_{\mathrm{train}}$ after applying the floor function.

As another sanity check, we can observe what happens if we allow the acceleration to increase without bound. We have egin{equation} \lim_{a o\infty} \widetilde{N}( au) = rac{T}{ au}. \end{equation} Thus, in the idealized infinite-acceleration model, the integer throughput is $\left\lfloor T/ au ight floor$. This makes sense because with infinite acceleration, the only bottleneck for the number of cars getting through would be the length of the green light and each driver’s reaction time.

Further, as expected, we have egin{equation} \lim_{ au o \infty} N( au) = 0. \end{equation} The limit tells us that the integer throughput eventually vanishes, while the following asymptotic relation describes how quickly the expression before rounding approaches zero: egin{equation} \widetilde{N}( au) \sim rac{T}{ au}, \quad au o \infty, \end{equation} where $\sim$ means that the ratio of the left-hand side to the right-hand side approaches one.

Visualizing the uncapped model

Figure 1 shows the integer throughput as a function of reaction time for three green-light durations.

Figure 1. $N( au)$ for $T=20,30,$ and $40\,\mathrm{s}$, with $L=5\,\mathrm{m}$ and $a=2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

Subtracting each curve in Figure 1 from its train benchmark gives the train advantage shown in Figure 2.

Figure 2. The train advantage $N_{\mathrm{train}}-N( au)$ for $T=20,30,$ and $40\,\mathrm{s}$, with $L=5\,\mathrm{m}$ and $a=2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. The corresponding train throughputs are $80$, $180$, and $320$ cars.

To factor out the different train throughputs, Figure 3 shows the ratio $N( au)/N_{\mathrm{train}}$.

Figure 3. The relative efficiency $N( au)/N_{\mathrm{train}}$ for $L=5\,\mathrm{m}$, $a=2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, and $T=20\,\mathrm{s}$.

Only the $T=20\,\mathrm{s}$ curve is shown in the relative efficiency plot because the curves for the other green-light durations have the same overall shape and would make the staircase plot harder to read. Their similarity does not mean that the efficiency is exactly independent of $T$. Dividing by $N_{\mathrm{train}}$ removes much of the change in scale, so the relative efficiency varies less dramatically than the absolute throughput over the range plotted. For sufficiently large $T$, however, the uncapped train throughput grows like $T^2$, while $\widetilde{N}( au)$ grows approximately like $T/ au$ at fixed positive $ au$. The uncapped relative efficiency must therefore eventually decrease as $T$ increases.

Several features stand out. The throughput is particularly sensitive to small reaction times because the delay accumulates down the line: car $n$ loses $n au$ seconds. For $T=20\,\mathrm{s}$, increasing the reaction time from zero to one second reduces the number of cars from $80$ to $12$, only $15\%$ of the ideal train throughput. As $ au$ increases further, the curve flattens because the system is already dominated by reaction delay.

Figures 4 and 5 give two complementary views of the same model: the first varies both $ au$ and $T$, while the second follows individual cars through time.

Figure 4. The integer-valued throughput across reaction time $ au$ and green-light duration $T$, with $L=5\,\mathrm{m}$ and $a=2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
Figure 5. A space-time diagram for $L=5\,\mathrm{m}$, $a=2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, $T=20\,\mathrm{s}$, and $ au=1\,\mathrm{s}$. Each curve is a car's rear-bumper position: it stays flat until that driver reacts, then bends upward as the car accelerates. A car passes if its curve reaches $x=x_0$ before the green light ends. Car $12$ is the last to pass, while car $13$ is the first to miss.

Figure 4 shows how longer green lights increase the absolute throughput, while Figure 5 makes the mechanism behind the reaction-time penalty visible. Each successive car remains stationary longer than the one ahead of it, producing a wave of delayed motion that propagates backward through the line. At fixed positive $ au$, the continuous threshold eventually grows approximately like $T/ au$, whereas the train result grows like $T^2$. The resulting gap is dramatic, but its size should not be interpreted as a realistic traffic-engineering prediction: it depends heavily on our assumption that the cars can accelerate indefinitely. Real cars have a maximum speed, so we turn to that extension next.

Adding a maximum speed

Motion of a speed-capped car

So far, each car has been allowed to accelerate forever. We now make the model more realistic by introducing a maximum speed $v_{\max}$. Let $t$ denote the time elapsed since a particular car begins moving. The car accelerates from rest at the constant acceleration $a$ until it reaches $v_{\max}$, then continues at that speed. The time required to reach the speed cap is egin{equation} t_a = rac{v_{\max}}{a}. \end{equation} The car’s velocity is therefore egin{equation} v(t) = egin{cases} at, & 0 \leq t \leq t_a, ewline v_{\max}, & t > t_a. \end{cases} \end{equation} Integrating the velocity gives the distance traveled. Before the car reaches its maximum speed, we recover the usual constant-acceleration result. Afterward, we add the distance traveled during the acceleration phase to the distance traveled while cruising: egin{align} d(t) &= egin{cases} \dfrac{1}{2}at^2, & 0 \leq t \leq t_a, ewline \dfrac{1}{2}at_a^2 + v_{\max}(t-t_a), & t > t_a \end{cases} ewline &= egin{cases} \dfrac{1}{2}at^2, & 0 \leq t \leq \dfrac{v_{\max}}{a}, ewline v_{\max}t-\dfrac{v_{\max}^2}{2a}, & t > \dfrac{v_{\max}}{a}. \end{cases} \end{align} Car $n$ begins moving at time $n au$, so it has $T-n au$ seconds to move before the light changes. Its rear bumper must travel $nL$, giving the condition egin{equation} d(T-n au) \geq nL. \end{equation}

Throughput with a speed cap

To solve this condition analytically, let $t_n$ denote the time that car $n$ must spend moving before its rear bumper reaches $x_0$. In other words, $d(t_n)=nL$. The distance traveled by the time the car first reaches $v_{\max}$ is egin{equation} d_a = rac{v_{\max}^2}{2a}. \end{equation} If $nL \leq d_a$, the car reaches $x_0$ while it is still accelerating, so egin{equation} t_n = \sqrt{ rac{2nL}{a}}. \end{equation} If $nL>d_a$, the car first accelerates for $t_a$ seconds and then travels the remaining distance $nL-d_a$ at $v_{\max}$. Therefore, egin{align} t_n &=t_a+ rac{nL-d_a}{v_{\max}} ewline &= rac{nL}{v_{\max}}+ rac{v_{\max}}{2a}. \end{align} Combining the two regimes gives egin{equation} t_n = egin{cases} \sqrt{\dfrac{2nL}{a}}, & nL \leq \dfrac{v_{\max}^2}{2a}, ewline \dfrac{nL}{v_{\max}}+\dfrac{v_{\max}}{2a}, & nL > \dfrac{v_{\max}^2}{2a}. \end{cases} \end{equation} Since the accumulated reaction delay is $n au$, car $n$ clears the light precisely when egin{equation} n au+t_n \leq T. \end{equation}

We can now solve for the largest car index. Define egin{equation} n_a = rac{d_a}{L} = rac{v_{\max}^2}{2aL}. \end{equation} Here $n_a$ is the continuous car index whose required travel distance $n_aL$ is exactly the acceleration distance $d_a$. It need not be an integer. The cutoff between the two regimes occurs when this car has exactly enough time to clear the light. Since it begins moving at time $n_a au$ and reaches $x_0$ after accelerating for $t_a$ seconds, the corresponding green-light duration is egin{equation} T_c = n_a au+t_a = rac{ au v_{\max}^2}{2aL}+ rac{v_{\max}}{a}. \end{equation}

Let $n^{\ast}( au)$ denote the largest continuous car index that satisfies the crossing condition, before applying the floor function. We obtain egin{equation} n^{\ast}( au)= egin{cases} \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{ rac{2L}{a}+4 au T}-\sqrt{ rac{2L}{a}}}{2 au} ight)^2, & T \leq T_c, ewline \dfrac{T- rac{v_{\max}}{2a}}{ au+ rac{L}{v_{\max}}}, & T>T_c. \end{cases} \end{equation} When $ au=0$ and the first branch applies, its expression is understood through its limit. The maximum speed throughput is egin{equation} N_{\mathrm{cap}}( au)=\left\lfloor n^{\ast}( au) ight floor. \end{equation}

The first branch is exactly our original answer. In this regime, the final car to clear the light reaches $x_0$ before reaching $v_{\max}$, so the speed cap never affects the motion relevant to the count. In the second regime, car $n$ reaches $x_0$ at time egin{equation} C_n=n au+t_n =n\left( au+ rac{L}{v_{\max}} ight)+ rac{v_{\max}}{2a}. \end{equation} The crossing times of two consecutive cars therefore differ by egin{equation} C_{n+1}-C_n= au+ rac{L}{v_{\max}}. \end{equation} The next car begins moving $ au$ seconds later and starts one additional car length from $x_0$, requiring another $L/v_{\max}$ seconds of cruising. The acceleration term is the same for both cars and cancels in the difference.

The capped train benchmark

For the train, every car begins moving at the same time. If $T\leq t_a=v_{\max}/a$, the train accelerates throughout the green light and travels $aT^2/2$, as before. If $T>t_a$, it first travels egin{equation} d_a= rac{1}{2}at_a^2= rac{v_{\max}^2}{2a} \end{equation} while accelerating. It then cruises at $v_{\max}$ for the remaining $T-t_a$ seconds. Its total distance in the second regime is therefore egin{align} d_{\mathrm{train}}(T) &=d_a+v_{\max}(T-t_a) ewline &= rac{v_{\max}^2}{2a} +v_{\max}\left(T- rac{v_{\max}}{a} ight) ewline &=v_{\max}T- rac{v_{\max}^2}{2a}. \end{align} Dividing the distance traveled by $L$ and rounding down gives egin{equation} N_{\mathrm{train,cap}} = egin{cases} \left\lfloor\dfrac{aT^2}{2L} ight floor, & T \leq \dfrac{v_{\max}}{a}, ewline \left\lfloor\dfrac{v_{\max}T- rac{v_{\max}^2}{2a}}{L} ight floor, & T>\dfrac{v_{\max}}{a}. \end{cases} \end{equation} Setting $ au=0$ in the car model therefore reproduces the capped-speed train result, just as it did in the original model.

Visualizing the capped model

The resulting capped throughput is shown in Figure 6 for three green-light durations.

Figure 6. $N_{\mathrm{cap}}( au)$ for $T=20,30,$ and $40\,\mathrm{s}$, with $L=5\,\mathrm{m}$, $a=2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, and $v_{\max}=15\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Figure 7 compares the capped result with the original unlimited-acceleration model.

Figure 7. The integer-valued capped and uncapped throughputs for $L=5\,\mathrm{m}$, $a=2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, $v_{\max}=15\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $T=20\,\mathrm{s}$. Once the curves coincide, the final car through the light never reaches the speed cap, so the original model applies unchanged.

Subtracting the capped car count from the capped train benchmark gives the train advantage in Figure 8.

Figure 8. The capped-speed train advantage $N_{\mathrm{train,cap}}-N_{\mathrm{cap}}( au)$ for $T=20,30,$ and $40\,\mathrm{s}$, with $L=5\,\mathrm{m}$, $a=2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, and $v_{\max}=15\,\mathrm{m/s}$. The corresponding capped train throughputs are $48$, $78$, and $108$ cars.

Figure 9 divides the car count by the capped train count to show the relative efficiency.

Figure 9. The relative efficiency $N_{\mathrm{cap}}( au)/N_{\mathrm{train,cap}}$ for $L=5\,\mathrm{m}$, $a=2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, $v_{\max}=15\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $T=20\,\mathrm{s}$.

Here too, only the $T=20\,\mathrm{s}$ efficiency curve is shown because the curves for $T=30$ and $40\,\mathrm{s}$ nearly overlap it. In the capped model, this overlap has a direct explanation. Once the cars and train spend most of the green light at $v_{\max}$, both throughputs grow linearly with $T$. Increasing the green-light duration can then add many cars to the absolute count without changing their relative efficiency very much.

For example, when $T=20\,\mathrm{s}$ and $ au=1\,\mathrm{s}$, $12$ cars clear the light compared with $48$ train cars. The speed cap lowers the ideal train benchmark from $80$ cars in the uncapped model to $48$, but the accumulated reaction delays still reduce the line to one quarter of that benchmark.

Finally, for a sufficiently long green light, both the car line and the train spend most of their time traveling at $v_{\max}$. Ignoring the negligible effect of the floor function on the leading-order behavior, their throughputs satisfy egin{align} n^{\ast}( au) &\sim rac{T}{ au+L/v_{\max}}, ewline N_{\mathrm{train,cap}} &\sim rac{v_{\max}T}{L}. \end{align} Since the floor function changes each continuous count by less than one, it does not affect the limiting ratio. Consequently, the relative efficiency of the actual integer throughputs satisfies egin{equation} \lim_{T o\infty} rac{N_{\mathrm{cap}}( au)}{N_{\mathrm{train,cap}}} = rac{L}{L+v_{\max} au}. \end{equation} Unlike the unlimited-acceleration model, both throughputs now grow linearly with $T$.

Heat map and space-time diagram

Figures 10 and 11 show how the capped model changes across parameter values and along individual vehicle trajectories.

Figure 10. The integer-valued capped throughput across reaction time $ au$ and green-light duration $T$, with $L=5\,\mathrm{m}$, $a=2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, and $v_{\max}=15\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
Figure 11. A capped-speed space-time diagram for $L=5\,\mathrm{m}$, $a=2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, $v_{\max}=15\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $T=30\,\mathrm{s}$, and $ au=1\,\mathrm{s}$. Each trajectory is initially curved while the car accelerates and becomes straight after it reaches $v_{\max}$. Car $19$ is the last to pass, while car $20$ is the first to miss.

The heat map in Figure 10 shows that longer green lights produce much larger absolute gains when reaction times are small. As $ au$ increases, accumulated reaction delay becomes the dominant bottleneck, so adding the same number of seconds to $T$ allows fewer additional cars through. The space-time diagram in Figure 11 makes the transition to cruising visible car by car: unlike the parabolic trajectories in the uncapped model, each path eventually straightens once its slope reaches $v_{\max}$. The maximum speed extension therefore preserves the clean zero reaction time correspondence while giving the long green light behavior a more realistic interpretation.

Conclusion

Reaction time accumulates down the queue, so the $n$th car loses $n au$ seconds before it begins moving. Treating the cars as a train removes this backward propagating delay, which explains both the train’s throughput advantage and the exact correspondence obtained when $ au=0$. The uncapped speed model makes this mechanism especially transparent, while the capped speed extension gives the long green light behavior a more realistic structure. In its cruising regime, each additional car effectively costs $ au+L/v_{\max}$ seconds, and the relative efficiency approaches the finite limit $L/(L+v_{\max} au)$.

We have assumed that every driver has the same deterministic reaction time $ au$. A natural stochastic extension would assign driver $k$ a random reaction time $R_k$, making the accumulated delay through car $n$ the random sum $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^n R_k$. The number of cars that clear the light would then be a random first-passage quantity rather than a single deterministic count. Its distribution could reveal the variability and tail risk in traffic throughput and show how correlations between drivers change the likelihood of an unusually good or bad cycle.

entry.title: My Favorite Derivation of the Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality

link.title: My Favorite Derivation of the Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality

entry.content:
Let $\mathbf{v,w} \in V$, a real inner product space. Consider the quadratic polynomial $p(t)$ defined as the inner product of the vector $\mathbf{v} + t\mathbf{w}$ with itself over $t \in \mathbb{R}$:

\begin{equation} p(t) = \braket{\mathbf{v} + t\mathbf{w}, \mathbf{v} + t\mathbf{w}}. \end{equation}

Since $p(t) \geq 0$, its discriminant must be nonpositive. This yields the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality: \begin{align} p(t) &= t^2 \lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert^2 + 2t \braket{\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}} + \lVert \mathbf{v}\rVert^2 \newline \implies \Delta(p(t)) &= 4\braket{\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}}^2 - 4 \lVert \mathbf{v} \rVert^2\lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert^2 \leq 0 \newline \implies |\braket{\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}}| &\leq \lVert \mathbf{v} \rVert\lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert. \end{align}

I found this derivation in an excellent book on this and other inequalities titled The Cauchy-Schwarz Master Class: An Introduction to the Art of Mathematical Inequalities by John Michael Steele.

entry.title: Point Mass on a Curve
entry.content:
For my first technical post, I’ll share a classical mechanics problem that I thought of while not fully paying attention during a lecture a while ago. I caught the physics bug while taking AP Physics 1 (classical mechanics) in junior year of high school, so I thought this would be an appropriate way to start.

A point mass $m$ travels along the smooth function $y(x): \mathbb{R} o \mathbb{R}$ under gravity and friction. Find the equation of motion for this particle.

I'm imagining a point mass using this curve $y(x)$ as a slide. For instance, take $y(x) = \sin(x) / x$; the figure below shows the particle placed at the point $(a, \sin(a)/a)$, ready to be released so we can observe its subsequent motion. Our goal is to find the governing differential equation of this motion. We will account for both the static and kinetic coefficients of friction. We ignore air resistance.

The setup: a point mass placed at rest at $(a, \sin(a)/a)$ on the slide $y(x) = \sin(x)/x$ (here $a = 1.5$), ready to be released.

Equation of motion derivation: frictionless case

To solve this problem, we turn to Lagrangian mechanicsIncidentally, for a long time, I was led to believe that Lagrangian mechanics cannot be applied to systems with nonconservative forces. That is certainly false, as we will see shortly. Incidentally, on a deeper level it is also true that there is no such thing as a nonconservative force. See here: https://www.feynmanlectures.caltech.edu/I_14.html.. This might be opening a can of worms if you have not seen Lagrangian mechanics before. For a good introduction to this topic, see this Feynman lecture. Please note that in this lecture, Feynman does not mention the dissipation function, which we will need here due to the frictional force. Also, I found an extremely helpful forum post which has the answer to my question. However, I feel that this person’s response could be made clearer. There is no mention of the dissipation function or radius of curvature. Even if I do not go into depth on certain topics, I think it is helpful to at least mention them explicitly so that someone who is interested has specific search terms that they can use to look into things further. Apart from that, there is a sign error in an intermediate step (on the potential energy) and there is a simplification that can be made for a certain term involving the signum function. That being said, I want to reiterate that this person’s answer was very useful and I was able to use it to check my own final answer.

To make the solution method a little more digestible, let’s begin with the frictionless case. In this case, we only need to take note of the functional known as the “action,” defined by egin{equation} S[q(t)] = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} L(q(t), \dot{q}(t),t)~\mathrm{d}t, \end{equation} where $q(t): \mathbb{R} o \mathbb{R}$Here I'm assuming $q(t): \mathbb{R} o \mathbb{R}$ because we are only concerned with a single particle's $x$-coordinate (i.e., $q(t) = x(t)$) but we could certainly also have the vectorized version $\vec{q}(t): \mathbb{R} o \mathbb{R}^n$ to keep track of several particles in multiple dimensions. describes the motion of the particle in generalized coordinates These are the specific set of coordinates used for the problem at hand. We will be using Cartesian coordinates but for a different problem (e.g., those involving a pendulum) polar coordinates may be more appropriate, for example. as a function of time $t$, $L$ is the Lagrangian, and we have used Newton’s dot notation to denote differentiation with respect to time. Further, we are assuming our observation takes place over the time interval $[t_0, t_1]$.

Why do we care about this action thing? Well, whatever mechanism that created the universe that we live in decided that between the points $x(t_0) = x_0$ and $x(t_1) = x_1$, the particle will follow the trajectory $x(t)$ for which the action $S$ is stationary, i.e., $\delta S = 0$. Despite having known this for about 8 years now, I still find this principle a bit magical. The principle of least action is equivalent to Newton’s second law, but then you might say it is also not obvious why the second law should be in the form that it is. (Why is it so simple? Why is it a second order differential equation? Why not third order? Fourth? It could have been an integro-differential equation. It could have been nonlinear. The possibilities are endless.) Again, it appears that these are simply the rules of the game that have been laid out, and what’s left for us to do is to play by them, however magical they may seem. We don’t ask why the bishop moves diagonally or why the knight jumps in the shape of an “L”; we play chess!

In classical mechanics, the Lagrangian takes a simple formTo stress the point, let me clearly state that this Lagrangian is specifically for classical mechanics. If we were dealing with electromagnetism for example, the Lagrangian would be something else (albeit similar).: it is the kinetic energy of the particle minus its potential energy. Plugging this in, we have egin{equation} S[x(t)] = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} rac{1}{2} m |\vec{v}|^2 - mgy ~\mathrm{d}t\end{equation} where we have switched from $q(t)$ to $x(t)$ to show that the generalized coordinate we’re using is the position along the $x$-axis in Cartesian coordinates, $\vec{v} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ is the particle velocityTherefore $|\vec{v}|$ is speed., $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity at sea level, and $y$ is the height of the particle as defined in the problem statement. In the interest of cleaner notation, we have suppressed the dependence of $v$ and $y$ on $x(t)$, but this dependence should be obvious from context. From this post onward, you can safely assume we are working with metric units unless I lose my mind and switch to something else, in which case I will point it out. Knowing that we’re using metric units, you can see that the Lagrangian has units of joules and that the action has units of joule-seconds. To find the path for which the action is stationary, we use variational calculus. I can make a post on that if requested.

Variational calculus tells us that the $x(t)$ for which $S$ is stationary should satisfy the Euler-Lagrange equation, egin{equation} \label{EL} rac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} rac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{x}} - rac{\partial L}{\partial x} = 0. \end{equation} As stated, the Lagrangian for our problem is simply the kinetic energy minus the potential energy. The kinetic energy is egin{align} rac{1}{2} m |\vec{v}|^2 &= rac{1}{2} m (v_x^2 + v_y^2), \end{align} where $v_x$ is the velocity in the $x$-direction and $v_y$ is the velocity in the $y$-direction. Since $x(t)$ is the $x$-coordinate of the position of the particle, $v_x$ is simply $\dot{x}(t)$. Similarly, $v_y$ is $\dot{y}(t)$, which we can write in terms of $\dot{x}(t)$ by using the chain rule, yielding $\dot{y}(t) = rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\dot{x}(t)$. Therefore, egin{align} \vec{v} &= \dot{x} egin{bmatrix} 1 ewline rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} \end{bmatrix} ewline \implies |\vec{v}|^2 &= \dot{x}^2\left[1 + \left( rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} ight)^2 ight] \end{align}

Meanwhile, the potential energy is $mgy$. Therefore, the Lagrangian is egin{equation} \label{lagrangian} L = rac{1}{2}m\dot{x}^2\left[1 + \left( rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} ight)^2 ight] - mgy.\end{equation} Now we compute the different terms in the Euler-Lagrange equation: egin{align} rac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{x}} &= m \dot{x}\left[1 + \left( rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} ight)^2 ight] ewline \implies rac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} rac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{x}} &= m \ddot{x}\left[1 + \left( rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} ight)^2 ight] + 2m\dot{x}^2 rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} rac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2}\end{align} and egin{equation} rac{\partial L}{\partial x} = m \dot{x}^2 rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} rac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} - mg rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}. \end{equation} Plugging into \eqref{EL} and rearranging, we have

egin{equation} \ddot{x} = - rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} rac{g + \dot{x}^2 rac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2}}{1 + \left( rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} ight)^2}. \label{frictionless} \end{equation}

Awesome! We now have a compact description of how a particle would traverse the frictionless curve $y(x)$. This is an autonomous,There is no explicit $t$ dependence. explicit,The highest order term $\ddot{x}$ is isolated on one side and written as a function of the independent variable, the dependent variable, and lower-order derivatives. nonlinear,It contains $\dot{x}^2$. second-orderThe highest number of derivatives we take of the unknown function $x(t)$ is two. ordinaryThere is only one independent variable $t$. differential equation. You might say that the position of the particle as a function of time is described by $x(t)$ (and $y(x(t))$) which is not what we have here. That may be true, but we can solve \eqref{frictionless} numerically for $x(t)$. I used the SciPy (a Python library) ODE integrator called $ exttt{solve\_ivp}$ to create the figures for this post. See the figure below for a point particle traversing a frictionless parabola.

A point mass sliding on the frictionless parabola $y = x^2$, released from rest at $x = -2$. With no energy lost, it oscillates forever.

Only for a very simple curve $y(x)$ could we ever hope to get a closed-form solution for $x(t)$. For $y(x) = x$, $\dot{x}(0) = 0$, $x(0) = 0$, we obtain $x(t) = -gt^2/4$ (and therefore $y(t) = -gt^2/4$). Let’s do a couple of sanity checks. For one, these expressions have the correct units of meters, since $g$ has units of meters per seconds squared and $t^2$ has units of seconds squared, giving meters once multiplied together. Also, as $t$ increases, notice that $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ become increasingly negative. That’s exactly what we should expect if we place the particle at the origin on the curve $y(x) = x$. It should slide down and to the left,Provided the static friction is low enough to permit the particle to start moving from rest, of course. which is exactly what our expressions for $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ are telling us. The velocity of the particle is also becoming increasingly negative in both components which is also to be expected since the particle is under the influence of gravity. One interesting feature of \eqref{frictionless} is that it is independent of the particle’s mass.

Adding friction

Now let’s return to the original problem, which involves friction. To handle that, we need to modify \eqref{EL}. Allow me to pull a couple more fast ones on you (the first one was the concept of “action”). First, we need to insert a “generalized force” on the right-hand side and second, we will need to find a coefficient of this generalized force. A generalized force is one that is defined over generalized coordinates. We have already specified that we will be working with the generalized coordinate $x(t)$ here and so the generalized force we will add is in terms of this. It might feel pedantic that I’m calling it a “generalized force” and not just a “force” but I want to use the proper terms so that you will have some familiarity with them already if you decide to read further and come across them. Otherwise, they might seem rather alien and you might feel cheated by my current usage of Lagrangian mechanics if you saw those terms in the wild but not here.

As stated, let’s add a generalized force on the right-hand side of \eqref{EL} egin{equation} \label{modified} rac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} rac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{x}} - rac{\partial L}{\partial x} = Q, \end{equation} where egin{equation} Q = - rac{\partial D}{\partial \dot{x}},~ D = rac{1}{N_v+1}\sum_{k} c_k |\vec{v_k}|^{N_v+1} \end{equation} are the generalized force and dissipation function, respectively. This is the modification that will allow us to handle dissipative forces in the Lagrangian formalism. The sum is over the $k$ objects in a system so for this problem, we will only retain one term. Further, $N_v$ is the order of the velocity dependence for the friction we are considering. In our case, we are not considering velocity-dependent friction the way we would have to if we were considering air resistance, for example. Therefore, $N_v=0$. We already found $\vec{v}$ (I’m suppressing the subscript because we only have one object) earlier and used it in \eqref{lagrangian}. Using that same $\vec{v}$, we find $D = c|\dot{x}|\sqrt{1 + ( rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x})^2}$. Plugging this into \eqref{modified}, we have egin{equation} \label{modified2} rac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} rac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{x}} - rac{\partial L}{\partial x} = -c\mathrm{sgn}(\dot{x})\sqrt{1 + \left( rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} ight)^2}\end{equation} for $\dot{x} eq 0$. The $\dot{x} = 0$ case requires us to consider static friction, which we will discuss shortly.

Let’s do some dimensional analysis. On the left-hand side of \eqref{modified2}, we have the term $ rac{\partial L}{\partial x}$. As stated earlier, the Lagrangian has units of joules. Therefore, this term has units of joules per meter, or newtons. That implies the right-hand side must also have units of newtons and they must be contained in the $c$ term, since $\sqrt{1 + ( rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x})^2}$ is unitless. This is the third and final fast one I will pull: $c$ is the force of friction. Of course, friction had to show up somewhere and $c$ has units of force so it feels morally correct to put them together but it is reasonable to question why $c$ is exactly equal to friction. It could have been some dimensionless constant times the force of friction, where that constant is not equal to one. Yet, that is not the case. At this point, I have to confess my ignorance. Please enlighten me if you have an explanation for this. Allow me to set $c = F_{\mu_k}$ to denote this relationship and move onward.

Free-body diagram at the mass. The track's local tangent (the incline) meets the horizontal at angle $ heta$, so the weight $mg$ resolves into $mg\cos heta$ perpendicular to the track and $mg\sin heta$ along it. The normal force $N$ is perpendicular to the surface.

Friction is proportional to the normal force, where the proportionality constant is the friction coefficient, i.e., $F_{\mu_k} = \mu_k N$. So now the task is to determine $N$. To do this, we need to recall the topic of uniform circular motion: when an object is constrained to move on a circular path at constant speed. Let’s pretend for a moment that our particle is undergoing uniform circular motion. Then, building on the free body diagram above, we find the relationship egin{equation} \label{normal} N - (mg)_{\perp} = rac{m|\vec{v}|^2}{r}, \end{equation} where $(mg)_{\perp}$ is the component of gravity perpendicular to the circular path and pointing away from the center of the circle and $r$ is the radius. Some simple trigonometry reveals that $(mg)_{\perp} = mg\cos( heta)$, where $ heta$ is the angle the particle makes with the horizontal. It is exactly the same angle $ heta$ you would find in a standard inclined plane problem. Another trigonometric fact we need is that $ an( heta)$ is exactly equal to $ rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$. This holds for any reasonable $y(x)$, not just a circular arc. Therefore, after writing $\cos( heta)$ in terms of $ an( heta)$, we have egin{equation} \cos( heta) = rac{1}{\sqrt{1 + \left( rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} ight)^2}}. \end{equation} That takes care of $(mg)_{\perp}$, and we would have everything we need to find the normal force if the particle was moving along a circular trajectory with radius $r$. However, we want an expression for the normal force (and therefore friction) to hold for a more general $y(x)$, not just one that traces out a circular arc. For a more general $y(x)$, we can treat the curve locally as part of a circular arc. In other words, if we zoom in enough, the particle appears to be traversing along a circle and from one point to the next along $y(x)$, it is traversing along circles of different radii. As an extreme example, even if the particle were traveling in a straight line, we could still treat it as traversing on a circular arc; one with infinite radius. Hopefully, this makes some sense intuitively but is there a way to properly quantify the radius associated with each point of $y(x)$? The answer is yes (or else we would be in trouble and I would have to end this post here)! Borrowing from differential geometry, the signed radius of curvature we want is egin{equation} r = rac{(1 + ( rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x})^2)^{ rac{3}{2}}}{ rac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2}}. \end{equation} The sign here is important. The numerator is always positive, so $r$ inherits the sign of $ rac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2}$: it is positive in a concave-up valley (where the center of the osculating circle sits above the track) and negative on a concave-down hilltop (where the center sits below). Keeping this sign is what lets a single expression for the normal force describe both cases correctly—on a hilltop it flips the centripetal term, which is exactly what will let the particle fly off the track later on. And with that, we have everything we need to find the normal force. Rearranging \eqref{normal} and plugging in what we just found, we have egin{align} N = m rac{g + \dot{x}^2 rac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2}}{\sqrt{1 + \left( rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} ight)^2}}.\end{align}

We now have everything we need to plug into \eqref{modified2}, which yields egin{align} m\ddot{x}\left[1 + \left( rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} ight)^2 ight] + m\dot{x}^2 rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} rac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} + mg rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} &= -\mu_k N \mathrm{sgn}(\dot{x})\sqrt{1+\left( rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} ight)^2} ewline &= -\mu_k m \mathrm{sgn}(\dot{x})\left(g + \dot{x}^2 rac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} ight).\end{align} After rearranging, we have

egin{equation} \ddot{x} = - rac{ \left(g + \dot{x}^2 rac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} ight) \left( rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} + \mu_k\,\mathrm{sgn}(\dot{x}) ight) }{ 1 + \left( rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} ight)^2 }. \label{frictionEOM} \end{equation}

Nice! We now have a compact description of the particle motion for the more difficult case where we take friction into account. If we plug in $\mu_k = 0$, we get back to the frictionless equation of motion given by \eqref{frictionless}, as we should. As in the frictionless case, \eqref{frictionEOM} is also independent of the particle’s mass.

Energy dissipation

It is useful to check what friction is doing to the particle’s mechanical energy. The total mechanical energy is egin{equation} E = rac{1}{2}m\dot{x}^2\left[1+\left( rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} ight)^2 ight] + mgy. \end{equation} Taking the time derivative and using the chain rule gives egin{align} rac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm{d}t} &= m\dot{x}\ddot{x}\left[1+\left( rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} ight)^2 ight] +m\dot{x}^3 rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} rac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} +mg\dot{x} rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} ewline &= m\dot{x}\left[ \ddot{x}\left(1+\left( rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} ight)^2 ight) +\dot{x}^2 rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} rac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} +g rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} ight]. \end{align} Substituting \eqref{frictionEOM} into this expression, the terms arising from gravity and the curvature of the track cancel, leaving egin{equation} rac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm{d}t} = -m\mu_k|\dot{x}| \left( g+\dot{x}^2 rac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} ight). \end{equation} Recall that we found the normal force to be egin{equation} N = m rac{g+\dot{x}^2 rac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2}} {\sqrt{1+\left( rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} ight)^2}}, \end{equation} while the speed of the particle is egin{equation} |\vec{v}| = |\dot{x}|\sqrt{1+\left( rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} ight)^2}. \end{equation} Therefore,

egin{equation} rac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\mu_k N|\vec{v}| \leq 0. \end{equation}

In other words, kinetic friction monotonically removes mechanical energy from the particle. This gives us an energetic explanation for the decaying oscillations we will see in the numerical solutions below.

What happens at rest?

Back at the start I promised we would account for static friction, so let’s make good on that. The key realization is that the equation of motion \eqref{frictionEOM} only describes the particle while it is moving. But what about the instants when the particle is momentarily at rest, like the top of a swing or the very moment we release it? That is the domain of static friction, and notice that it appears nowhere in \eqref{frictionEOM}.

Kinetic friction has a fixed magnitude $\mu_k N$ and always points against the motion. Static friction is instead a reaction force: it supplies exactly as much force as needed to prevent sliding, up to a ceiling of $\mu_s N$.

So static friction poses exactly one new question: at a moment of rest, does the particle stay put or begin to slide? We answer it with a force balance. At rest there is no centripetal term, so the normal force is just $N = mg\cos( heta)$. Gravity’s pull along the track is $mg\sin( heta)$, directed downhill. To keep the particle still, static friction must cancel that pull, which it can do only up to its ceiling: egin{equation} mg\sin( heta) \le \mu_s\, mg\cos( heta) \implies an( heta) \le \mu_s. \end{equation} Since we already found that $ an( heta) = rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$, the condition to stay stuck is wonderfully simple: egin{equation} \left\lvert rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} ight vert \le \mu_s. \end{equation} The particle sticks wherever the slope is shallow enough. This is the classic angle of friction: the steepest angle $ heta_{\max} = \arctan(\mu_s)$ at which static friction can still hold. Wherever $\left\lvert rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} ight vert > \mu_s$, the particle must slide, and \eqref{frictionEOM} takes over.

The points where $\left\lvert rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} ight vert \le \mu_s$ form resting bands along the curve, and these bands are the only places the particle can ever come to rest. The reason is simple: if the particle reaches zero velocity while inside a band, static friction is strong enough to hold it and it stays put for good; if it stops anywhere else, the slope beats static friction and it immediately slides on.With $\mu_s = 0$ these bands collapse to just the exact stationary points ($ rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 0$), and the particle would creep infinitely slowly toward the very bottom, never quite settling in finite time. Turning $\mu_s$ on is exactly what makes the "it comes to rest" story clean. For the figures below I take $\mu_s = \mu_k$, a common simplification. If we set the particle down at rest inside a band, it never moves.

To make the resting bands concrete, here they are drawn on the $\sin(x)/x$ slide. The shaded strips mark every stretch shallow enough that static friction could hold the particle at rest. They widen around the flat troughs and crests and pinch to nothing on the steep descents.

The resting bands on $y = \sin(x)/x$ (here $\mu_s = 0.1$), shaded where $\left\lvert rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} ight vert \le \mu_s$. The particle can only come to rest on the bolded stretches; everywhere else the slope is too steep and it must keep sliding.

Numerics

With the physics in hand, let’s watch it happen. The animation below puts the same particle on the parabola $y = x^2$, released from rest at the same spot, once without friction and once with. Without friction it swings from side to side forever; with friction it bleeds off energy on every pass and eventually comes to rest.

The same release on $y = x^2$: frictionless (left) versus with friction (right, $\mu_k = \mu_s = 0.2$). The frictionless ball oscillates forever; the frictional one decays and comes to rest.

Plotting the $x$-coordinate over time makes the decay explicit. A larger friction coefficient damps the motion faster, and each run comes to rest inside its dead band.

$x(t)$ for a few friction coefficients. $\mu_k = 0$ oscillates undamped; larger $\mu_k$ causes faster decay.

Leaving the track

So far we’ve quietly assumed the particle stays glued to the curve. But a slide can only push—it can’t pull the particle down onto itself. So the normal force must satisfy $N \ge 0$. Recall that we found egin{equation} N = m\, rac{g + \dot{x}^2 rac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2}}{\sqrt{1+\left( rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} ight)^2}}. \end{equation} The mass and the denominator are positive, so the sign of $N$ is just the sign of $g + \dot{x}^2 rac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2}$. On a concave-up stretch ($ rac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} > 0$, the inside of a valley) that is always positive and all is well. But on a concave-down stretch ($ rac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} < 0$, the crest of a hill), a fast-enough particle demands more centripetal force than gravity can provide; $N$ would have to turn negative to keep it down, and since the track cannot pull, the particle leaves the surface and sails off as a projectile. The condition to stay on the track is simply egin{equation} g + \dot{x}^2 rac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} \ge 0. \end{equation}

This is the same reason a roller coaster throws you out of your seat over a hill taken too fast, and it becomes a genuine constraint once we go hunting for more interesting curves. Consider a double-well quartic, $y = 0.1x^4 - 0.4x^2$: two valleys with a hill between them. Released from one side, with the friction, quartic coefficients, and initial height all chosen appropriately, the particle rolls over the central hill and settles in the far valley, staying on the track the whole way. Change those parameters—dropping it from higher, say—and it is possible that it would fly off at the hill instead.I checked numerically that the particle shown keeps $g + \dot{x}^2 rac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} \ge 0$ for its entire trip, so it never actually leaves the track.

A double-well quartic $y = 0.1x^4 - 0.4x^2$, with the particle released from the left arm.
With $\mu_k = \mu_s = 0.05$, the particle rolls over the central hill and settles in the right well, staying on the track the whole way.

Phase space

Let’s take another way of seeing the same motion. Instead of watching the particle on the curve, we plot its state in the phase plane: position $x$ on one axis, momentum on the other. Which momentum? The natural choice is one we have already met, the canonical momentum conjugate to $x$, which is exactly the quantity $ rac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{x}}$ we computed on the way to the Euler-Lagrange equation, egin{equation} p = rac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{x}} = m\dot{x}\left[1 + \left( rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} ight)^2 ight]. \end{equation}

A single point $(x, p)$ captures the entire state of the particle, and as time runs that point traces out a curve. Without friction, energy is conserved, so the particle is pinned to a constant energy contour and its phase-space curve is a closed loop, retracing the same orbit forever. With friction, energy leaks away, the particle can no longer close its loop, and instead it spirals inward: each loop is smaller than the one before, winding in until the motion comes to rest. Energy loss, which we found leaks away at rate $\mu_k N\lvert\vec{v} vert$, becomes visible as the steady shrinking of the orbit’s loops.Recall that the trajectory itself does not depend on the mass, so for the figure I simply set $m = 1$.

The figure below shows this for the double-well quartic. The gray loop is the frictionless orbit the particle would trace forever; the colored curve (shaded by time) is the real, frictional trajectory, peeling off that loop and spiraling in to rest inside the right-hand side well.

The quartic run in the phase plane. Gray: the frictionless closed orbit. Colored (dark to light with time): the frictional trajectory spiraling in to rest inside the right well.

We also observe the $\sin(x)/x$ slide from this perspective, shown below with its motion along the curve (top) playing in lockstep with its phase portrait (bottom). Under the given conditions, the particle does not oscillate in place; it makes one long rightward run, turns around a single time, and settles in a distant trough.

The $\sin(x)/x$ slide, the same run shown two ways in sync: motion on the curve (top) and in the phase plane (bottom). No spiral—just one broad sweep to rest.

Where to go from here

There are several extensions we can make to this problem.

  • An ant with a jetpack. Suppose that the particle is a tiny intelligent ant named Flik, who has his own jetpack. It provides him thrust tangential to the curve at any given point. Flik is an adventurer; he wants to reach as large an $x$-coordinate as possible. Suppose Flik wants to stay on the curve during his journey and that his jetpack has a finite fuel supply. Find the optimal policy on how to use the jetpack. This is an optimal control problem, and it would be interesting to see whether the optimal policy can be derived analytically. Alternatively, we could take a learning-based approach, such as reinforcement learning, and have Flik learn a strategy through trial and error.
  • Air resistance / velocity-dependent friction. We could include velocity-dependent air resistance and in that case we would require a dissipation function with $N_v e 0$.
  • Rolling instead of sliding. Here we assumed a point particle, which necessarily can only slide along the given function. We could instead consider an extended particle, which would have a moment of inertia and could roll along the curve.
  • From a curve to a surface $z(x,y)$. We could extend our one-dimensional study here to two dimensions.
  • Families of curves. We could try to classify families of curves for given initial conditions that allow the particle to reach a certain $x$-coordinate. It is obvious that if we were to release the particle from rest at a point where $ rac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} > 0$, it would never reach an $x$-coordinate to the right of that point. Then what are the conditions on $y(x)$ that do allow the particle to reach a prescribed destination?

entry.title: The Three-Body Problem
entry.content:
He remembered taking a class in information theory as a third-year student in college. The professor had put up two pictures: One was the famous Song Dynasty painting Along the River During the Qingming Festival, full of fine, rich details; the other was a photograph of the sky on a sunny day, the deep blue expanse broken only by a wisp of cloud that one couldn’t even be sure was there. The professor asked the class which picture contained more information. The answer was that the photograph’s information content—its entropy—exceeded the painting’s by one or two orders of magnitude.

Three Body was the same. Its enormous information content was hidden deep. Wang could feel it, but he could not articulate it. He suddenly understood that the makers of Three Body took the exact opposite of the approach taken by designers of other games. Normally, game designers tried to display as much information as possible to increase the sense of realism. But Three Body’s designers worked to compress the information content to disguise a more complex reality, just like that seemingly empty photograph of the sky.

— Liú Cíxīn, The Three-Body Problem

entry.title: What this is and what this isn’t

link.title: What this is and what this isn’t

entry.content:
In short, this is what it is and it’s not what it’s not. In other words, I don’t want to pigeonhole this into a specific category, although it may end up following some common theme(s). I don’t know. We’ll have to wait and see.

For now, I can tell you what I currently want to write about. I would like to share things from physics and math which I find interesting and/or useful. This will probably end up being a mix of elementary and advanced topics, but of course the difficulty level is subjective.

I would be really happy if someone found some entertainment and/or learned something new here but I also have selfish reasons for writing: this will help me organize my thoughts, force me to be clear and correct, clear up my own confusions, and leave me with references I can return to in the future. Terence Tao has a great post on this that resonates with me.

I expect that some posts will be more useful as references and others will prioritize pedagogy.

I should make a note on rigor. You should expect rigor in the flavor of a physicist or engineer rather than a mathematician. I want to be able to use the Dirac delta without invoking Schwartz’ work that put it on rigorous grounding; if it was good enough for Dirac to use before Schwartz, it’s good enough for me. I want to be able to exchange integrals and derivatives without anxiety. I do not want to spend time proving that the conditions for the dominated convergence theorem hold before switching limits and integrals. Maybe every now and then I’ll throw in something like that. I’ll share a relevant quote from the preface of Anthony Zee’s quantum field theory book:

Indeed, a Fields Medalist once told me that top mathematicians secretly think like physicists and after they work out the broad outline of a proof they then dress it up with epsilons and deltas [...] As we like to say in the theoretical physics community, too much rigor soon leads to rigor mortis. Be warned.

— Anthony Zee, Quantum Field Theory in a Nutshell, 2nd Edition

Having said that, I will strive to not be egregiously hand-wavy either. For any steps that I am not completely comfortable with, I will be honest and point those out as they arise instead of pretending hand-waviness makes sense. Consider those occurrences as invitations to enlighten me.

Anyway, as I said at the start, I want to be able to talk about a variety of topics here. So even if I begin with a bunch of physics and math, do not be surprised by movie recs, showerthoughts, etc..
